name: Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling
text:
# Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling


## Overview
Space skipping and empty volume culling are [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) techniques in image-order volume rendering that reduce computational load by identifying and bypassing regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image [S2][S4, unofficial]. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its primary focus on geometric or scalar-based determination of "visible" vs. "invisible" primitives (cells, voxels, or rays) before expensive integration occurs, whereas methods like [Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control](1791-early-termination-and-probabilistic-path-control.md) operate during the [ray-marching](#6739-ray-marching.md) process itself [G].

## Shared principles
Builds on the core acceleration mechanisms defined in [Acceleration](18-acceleration.md), which reduce work units through culling/skipping, termination, and adaptation [G].

## Subtopics

### [Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists](2565-parallel-ray-casting-with-segment-lists.md)
[Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists](#2565-parallel-ray-casting-with-segment-lists.md) is a distributed rendering algorithm that accelerates volume visualization by combining spatial culling via segment lists with multi-threaded and multi-process parallelism. It solves the performance bottleneck of [standard ray casting](#12643-standard-ray-casting.md) by pre-computing the entry and exit points of a ray through the volume's non-empty regions (segments), thereby skipping empty space entirely, and distributing the resulting pixel rows across MPI ranks and OpenMP threads. It differs from its siblings by explicitly managing job distribution across a cluster-like environment (MPI) and using a segment list data structure to define the integration bounds, whereas methods like [SparseLeap](5152-sparseleap.md) use sparse voxel octrees for [hierarchical traversal](#896-hierarchical-traversal.md).

### [SparseLeap](5152-sparseleap.md)
[SparseLeap](#5152-sparseleap.md) is a hybrid object-order (rasterization) and image-order (ray-casting) method for efficient [empty space skipping](#1002-empty-space-skipping.md) in large, sparse volumes with fine structures. It solves the problem of space fragmentation and hierarchy traversal overhead inherent in standard octree-based skipping by decoupling empty space detection from [volume sampling](#7111-volume-sampling.md). Unlike siblings that traverse a tree per ray, SparseLeap rasterizes occupancy geometry into per-pixel linked lists of ray segments, allowing the ray-caster to leap over empty space via simple linear list traversal.

### [Visibility Culling](6226-visibility-culling.md)
[Visibility culling](#6226-visibility-culling.md) reduces rendering workload by identifying and excluding primitives, voxels, or ray segments that do not contribute to the final image due to occlusion, spatial bounds, or negligible radiometric contribution. It differs from its siblings by encompassing a broad spectrum of techniques: from geometric rejection (e.g., [Frustum Culling](8463-frustum-culling.md), [24-Region View-Dependent Visibility Preprocessing](6608-24-region-view-dependent-visibility-preprocessing.md)) and occlusion testing (e.g., [Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map](990-occlusion-clipping-with-orthogonal-opacity-map.md), [Visibility Feedback with Screen Space Subdivision](3439-visibility-feedback-with-screen-space-subdivision.md)) to radiometric termination (e.g., [Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control](1791-early-termination-and-probabilistic-path-control.md)) and performance management (e.g., [Interactive Render Quality Estimation & Cancellation](8895-interactive-render-quality-estimation-cancellation.md)).

### [Efficient Space Skipping & Adaptive Sampling of Unstructured Volumes Using H.W. Accel. Ray Tracing](8217-efficient-space-skipping-adaptive-sampling-of-unstructured-v.md)
This method enables interactive visualization of large unstructured volumes (e.g., finite element simulation data) by leveraging hardware-accelerated ray tracing to accelerate acceleration structure traversal and point-in-element tests. It solves the bottleneck of traditional rasterization, which requires sorting 20–40 GB of unstructured elements front-to-back on every camera move. Unlike sibling methods that often assume [regular grids](#3-dense-grids-and-memory-layout.md), this approach works directly on unstructured meshes by partitioning them into convex disjoint regions, skipping transparent elements and voids, and adapting sampling rates based on local data variance.

### [SparseLeap Ray-Casting with Occupancy Misses](9818-sparseleap-ray-casting-with-occupancy-misses.md)
SparseLeap is a volume rendering acceleration technique that separates meta-data for empty space skipping from the volume data itself, using a ray-guided framework where ray segments are processed via a list. It extends standard ray-casting by introducing an outer loop over ray segments and handling 'occupancy misses' to delay the determination of whether a brick is empty or non-empty until it is actually needed. Unlike octree-based skipping which incurs high depth complexity due to fragmented space subdivision, SparseLeap limits depth complexity by generating a sparse list of ray segments, significantly reducing the number of traversal steps per ray.

### Parsimonious Ray Sampling and Fused Rendering
- **Definition:** A rendering optimization that infers [ray-BBox intersection](#772-ray-box-intersection.md) to sample query points only within the scene bounding box, applicable only to bounded scenes [S1, unofficial].
- **Steps:** Fuse approximately ten point-wise operations for the forward and backward pass of the [density-to-alpha](#3052-raw2alpha-density-to-alpha-conversion.md) function conversion [S1, unofficial]. In the volume rendering accumulation, halt tracking a ray once the accumulated transmittance falls below $10^{-3}$ [S1, unofficial].

### Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping
- **Definition:** A method for visualizing large-scale aerosols (smoke, fog, dust) by optimizing traditional [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md) to avoid sampling empty spaces and invalid voxels, reducing hardware load and improving speed [S2].
- **Steps:** Optimize and accelerate the traditional ray casting algorithm through the hierarchical bounding box tree [S2]. Combine an illumination model to enhance the color rendering of each voxel [S2].
- **Comparison:** Reduces unnecessary space debris to lower hardware load and improve rendering speed, meeting real-time rendering requirements for large-scale aerosols [S2].

### Surface Localization Acceleration
- **Definition:** Acceleration methods that localize the surface interface and concentrate samples only in relevant regions, effectively skipping empty space, because only 10-20% of evaluated samples have non-zero density [S3].
- **Steps:** Refine the sampling strategy to focus solely on the localized surface [S3].
- **Comparison:** Standard volumetric rendering is inefficient because it samples the entire ray; surface localization reduces the number of required MLP evaluations by skipping empty space [S3].

### Per-ray Volume Culling
- **Definition:** Optimization to avoid visiting every volume at every step. Previously, the march visited every volume at every step just to ask cell_index whether it was inside, and almost always was not. The new method builds an active list up front, so a step only visits volumes whose t-range contains it [S4, unofficial].
- **Comparison:** Differs from the previous approach which visited every volume at every step. The new approach is pure work elimination and produces byte-identical output [S4, unofficial].

## Background
Standard volumetric rendering is inherently inefficient because it samples the entire ray, even though surface geometry occupies only a fraction of the 3D space [S3]. As observed by Piala et al. [PC21] and Hu et al. [HLC∗ 22], only around 10 to 20% of the evaluated samples have non-zero density and actually contribute to the final image [S3]. To address this, acceleration methods aim to localize the surface interface and concentrate samples only in these relevant regions, effectively skipping empty space [S3]. Existing approaches generally fall into four categories based on how they define this region of interest: (1) using sparse data structures [SSC22], (2) leveraging depth oracles [NSP∗ 21,LPX∗ 22], (3) guiding sampling via [Signed Distance Fields](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md) [SZZ∗ 22,WRB∗ 23] or density estimates [HLC∗ 22], and (4) employing learned sampling networks [PC21,KNL∗ 22] [S3].

For large-scale aerosol visualization (smoke, fog, dust), traditional ray casting algorithms suffer from low efficiency, slow speed, and large resource consumption [S2]. A method proposed in [S2] optimizes the algorithm through a hierarchical bounding box tree to avoid sampling empty spaces and invalid voxels, combining this with an illumination model to enhance color rendering.

In unstructured volume rendering, traditional rasterization requires sorting 20–40 GB of unstructured elements front-to-back on every camera move [S1, unofficial]. Hardware-accelerated ray tracing is used to bypass this bottleneck by partitioning elements into convex disjoint regions and skipping transparent elements and voids [S1, unofficial].

For multi-volume scenes, per-ray volume culling builds an active list up front so that a step only visits volumes whose t-range contains it, eliminating unnecessary cell_index checks [S4, unofficial]. This pure work elimination produces byte-identical output while reducing [CPU](#10688-naive-sdf-generation-cpu.md) raycast times from 70.4 ms to 47.6 ms for 9 volumes at 640x360 resolution [S4, unofficial].
